anchors.extracted: Urn randomization balancing seven characteristics. Al-Anon facilitation: up to 12 sessions of 60 minutes, adapted from Project MATCH. Johnson Institute intervention: six sessions of about 2 hours, preparing the family to confront the drinker. CRAFT replicated and extended the approach tested by Sisson and Azrin (1986), originally developed by Robert J. Meyers (second author), who supervised this condition: awareness training, rewarding not drinking, communication skills, competing and outside activities, handling dangerous situations and suggesting counselling, all in individual sessions. All approaches manual-guided with about 12 hours of contact; therapists nested within approaches; CRAFT's five therapists had less experience (four with 0–3 years) than those in the other approaches.

anchors.extracted: Substituting a long-acting benzodiazepine before tapering has little evidence of efficacy, and the rate of taper rests on prescribers' clinical experience rather than good empirical evidence; with slow tapering about two-thirds of patients stop completely (no citation). Summary: withdrawal can be hazardous, with fits, psychosis and depression, and the outcome is usually favourable with tapered withdrawal, with a worse prognosis in elderly people. In high-dose use, tolerance sets in rapidly and withdrawal syndromes, sometimes severe with fits and psychotic reactions, can follow attempted stopping. No study comparing abrupt with gradual stopping for seizures is cited.

anchors.extracted: Abrupt cessation after 1–6 months of use can cause life-threatening seizures (no reference, no frequency). The Box (no source) lists general symptoms (headache, palpitations, sweating), tremor and muscle aches, neurological symptoms including confusion and delirium, particularly in older people, delusions, hallucinations and grand mal seizures 1–12 days after stopping, gastrointestinal symptoms, and psychological symptoms including rebound insomnia, anxiety and panic, perceptual distortions, depersonalization and depression.

anchors.extracted: Purpose-built national online survey (late 2015) with five written festival scenarios built from 114 Australian police media releases and news articles (2002–2014) and focus-group tested: high-visibility policing, riot policing, drug detection dogs, collaborative policing and no police (police said to have left before the band the respondent wants to see). Each participant was block-randomised to receive two scenarios and asked under each whether they would use, possess (carry into the grounds), buy inside, give or sell illicit drugs; those saying yes were asked which drugs and what quantity. 2,115 eligible respondents (of 2,137 asked about festivals), recruited mainly through youth, music and drug forums and social media; 506 to 561 per block.
